text:
**The Fourth Row**

Barbara Feld had stopped going to services sometime in her second trimester, when the walk from the parking lot began to feel like a referendum on her ankles. But her mother-in-law, Ruth, had called on Thursday to say that the Lowensteins' grandson was being honored that Saturday, and also that she hadn't seen Barbara in shul since Rosh Hashanah, and also, in the same breath, that she was only saying.

So on the twelfth of February, 1966, Barbara put on the navy maternity dress with the white collar, the one that made her look like an enormous schoolgirl, and let Leonard help her into the car. It was eleven degrees. The sky over Southfield was the color of a nickel. Leonard drove with both hands on the wheel, the way he did when carrying something fragile, which these days meant her.

"You'll sit on the aisle," he said. "In case you have to get up."

She was eight months and one week along. She had to get up all the time.

The sanctuary at Shaarey Zedek still struck her, four years after it opened, as a building designed by someone who wanted God to feel slightly underdressed. The roof rose to a point like a great folded hand, and the light came down through tall panes in long, cold columns.

Ruth had saved them seats in the fourth row. She kissed Barbara on both cheeks and put a hand on her stomach without asking, as though checking a cake.

"He's low," Ruth said. "It's a boy."

"You said that about Marilyn's, and she had Debbie."

"Marilyn carried wide."

Leonard opened his prayer book to the wrong page. Barbara found him the right one and he squeezed her hand. He was a kind man who did not like to be looked at, which was one of the reasons she had married him. He sold commercial insurance. He believed, deeply and without fuss, in contingency.

---

Rabbi Adler came out a little after ten. He was not a large man, but he seemed to stand at the center of whatever room he entered. Barbara's father used to clip his columns from the *Jewish News* on civil rights and on the danger of mistaking prosperity for virtue, and leave them folded on her pillow.

What she remembered most, though, was an afternoon at Camp Tamarack, the summer she was a counselor there. He had come to speak to the older campers, and afterward a boy in her cabin, a skinny, furious, brilliant twelve-year-old who corrected the arts-and-crafts instructor's grammar, followed the rabbi to his car and asked whether he thought God was embarrassed by people. The rabbi laughed, then stopped laughing and said, "Sometimes, I would think."

That boy used to sit with her at the waterfront after lights-out when he couldn't sleep, which was most nights, and talk about Spinoza and Hamlet and the Warsaw ghetto, about everything except whatever kept him awake. She had been nineteen. She thought what he needed was someone to listen, so she listened. At summer's end he gave her a list of books to read, written in a tiny, slanting hand, and she lost it, and felt bad about losing it for longer than made sense.

---

The service moved in its familiar tides: standing, sitting, the rustle of pages, the cantor's voice rising into the peak of the roof. The baby shifted, a slow rolling under her ribs, like someone turning over in a narrow bed. Leonard raised his eyebrows. *Fine*, she mouthed.

It was nearly eleven when a young man came up the steps of the bimah.

He was too thin for his suit, which hung from his shoulders as though borrowed. He held his paper in both hands, close to his chest, the way children hold a recital piece. Nobody went up there uninvited, and the whole room leaned forward a quarter of an inch in confusion.

He began to read, his voice high and very precise, something about hypocrisy, about a community grown fat and complacent. He said the words *a protest*. Somebody behind her said, "Who *is* that?" in the tone you'd use for a drunk at a wedding. An usher started toward the steps, unhurried.

And Barbara looked up at the young man's face and knew him.

The recognition came the way the cold comes when you open a door in winter, all at once and everywhere. The face had lengthened and hollowed, but the slant of the mouth was the same, and so was the terrible concentration she had seen at the waterfront at midnight, when he'd tried to explain why it mattered so much whether the universe was indifferent or merely busy.

She said his name. She didn't know if she said it aloud.

Then he took a gun out of his jacket.

---

What happened next has been written about many times, and Barbara has read most of it and recognized almost none of it. The accounts are orderly: the rabbi, the shots, the boy turning the gun on himself. One says the congregation "sat frozen," which is true for perhaps a second and a half and then completely untrue.

What she remembers isn't the gunshots, which were smaller than she would have guessed, like a book dropped on a table in another room. It is the sound after: a thousand people drawing breath at once, then the long tearing noise of everyone standing up.

She was already moving before the second shot. She remembers the strange lightness of it, as if the weight she'd carried for eight months had been lifted, and she was nineteen again on a dock in the dark and someone needed her. She stepped into the aisle, thinking, *If I can just get to him, if I can say his name close enough that he hears it.* She did not think about the gun. She thought only that he had always been talking to someone who wasn't listening, and that she had listened, once, for a whole summer, and maybe that counted for something.

Then the crowd came.

It was not malicious, not even exactly panic. It was a great body of people who had suddenly remembered that they could die, moving away, up the aisles, toward the doors where the cold light was. They came past her and into her, and she was turned like a stone in a stream. She saw a fur collar, an elbow, the gray back of a suit. She saw, for one instant between two shoulders, the rabbi down and people bending over him, and beyond them, a shape in a too-large suit that nobody was bending over at all.

She called the boy's name again. It was one sound in a room full of sounds.

Then Leonard had her arm, white as paper, saying *Barbara Barbara Barbara*, and Ruth, hatless, had the other, and her feet kept going backward up the aisle while her face stayed turned the other way. The baby kicked, hard, once. Then she was outside, and the air tasted like metal, and people stood in the snow without their coats, and one man kept saying, to no one, "In the shul. In the shul."

---

The rabbi lived for nearly a month. Barbara called the hospital twice and hung up both times before anyone answered. When he died, in March, she did not go to the funeral, because the baby was due any day, and because she was afraid that if she stood in that crowd again she would start walking the wrong way.

There was a small item in the paper about the young man's family, his time at the university, the hospitals. She folded it very small and put it in the drawer with the warranties and spare keys, where it stayed for thirty years.

Her son was born on the twenty-third of March. Ruth was right; he'd been low. When the nurse brought him, Barbara looked a long time at his face, red and furious and entirely new, and thought, absurdly, *I'll listen to you.* As if listening had ever been enough.

She told Leonard, eventually, that she had known the boy. He was quiet a while, then said, "You couldn't have reached him," and she understood he meant the aisle, the crowd, thirty feet. She let him mean that. It was simpler than explaining the other distance, the one that had opened years before on a dock in the dark, between a girl who thought listening was the same as hearing and a boy who had been trying to tell her something she was too young to understand.

When people learned she had been there, they asked what it was like, and she told them about the cold, the roof like a folded hand, the sound of everyone standing up. She never told them she had been walking forward. It seemed the kind of thing that would require a better ending than she had.
